FinanceTab.title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Fed governor Lisa Cook
FinanceTab.text:
Donald Trump announced on Friday that he is establishing a committee to investigate Lisa Cook, the US Federal Reserve governor, over allegations that she committed mortgage fraud, renewing his efforts to oust her despite a June supreme court ruling that her earlier firing was unconstitutional.

Trump said a committee will consult with justice department officials to decide whether there is “cause” for her removal. The White House will hold an in-person hearing on 5 November to consider the allegations against Cook, which will be closed to the public but transcribed and published. Cook will be able to submit a written statement to present her own evidence and will be subject to examination from White House and her own legal counsel.

“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a statement posted to the White House’s website.

Her legal team has maintained that the White House is “cherrypicking” facts and any claims of fraud are based on unrelated clerical errors.

In response to the announcement, Cook’s lawyers said that they had “grave doubts” that the White House hearing would be “a legitimate one that would conform to the law”.

“But if it is anything close to objective,” they continued, “the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board.”

They added that Cook “welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her”.

Cook was appointed by Joe Biden in 2022 to a 14-year term, becoming the Fed’s first Black governor. Before her tenure at the central bank, she taught at Harvard University and Stanford University and served on Barack Obama’s council of economic advisers.

Cook’s battle with the White House began in August 2025 when she was abruptly fired after Trump said she committed mortgage fraud by listing two properties in Georgia and Michigan as her primary residence and failing to report rental income on her Atlanta property.

Cook immediately sued the Trump administration, and the supreme court reinstated her after a 5-4 ruling that she could stay on as governor while fighting the fraud allegations.

In June, the court ruled that Trump’s firing was unconstitutional because he did not follow proper procedure and give Cook an opportunity to dispute the allegations before she was fired.

Cook was fired just as Trump was launching unprecedented attacks on the Fed’s chair, then Jerome Powell, in his blustering push to get the central bank to lower interest rates. Trump also launched a justice department investigation into Powell, which was dropped in April.

Congress created the Fed to be an independent and non-partisan institution. Economists widely agree that a central bank unswayed by politics is essential for the stability of a country’s economy.

Kevin Warsh, Powell’s successor, has repeatedly faced questions over how he will maintain the Fed’s independence. Before Trump picked him to lead the world’s most powerful central bank, he had echoed the president’s calls for cutting rates. But because of elevated inflation brought on by the war in the Middle East, the bank ultimately voted to raise rates in its last meeting, which drew the ire of the White House just more than a month before the crucial midterm elections.

FinanceTab.title: Trump immigrant purge could cut social security for Americans by $2,000 a year
FinanceTab.text:
Elderly Americans can expect to lose an average of $2,152 in annual social security benefits each, a projected 8.6% reduction in their retirement payments, by 2034 and every year after as a direct consequence of the economic fallout from the Trump administration’s anti-immigration campaign, if that carries on, according to a new report shared exclusively with the Guardian.

Already, US food prices are up, housing permits to build new homes are down – and even native-born Americans are losing out on potential jobs after the sudden exodus of 1.2 million foreign-born workers over the last two years as a result of Donald Trump’s policies, the report finds.

“When the Trump administration says things, it’s not always data-driven. And we wanted to see what the data shows, and what other people have found the data shows,” said Michael Ettlinger, one of the report’s authors. “Turns out that refutes what the US president primarily is asserting.”

The blowback on the economy from Donald Trump’s crackdown is wide-ranging, even as the federal government’s aggressive mass deportation campaign quietly ramps up further.

“We are just beginning to see the harms in terms of what is happening here domestically. But the impacts of these policies, of these efforts, are going to be long-lasting. And I think that is by design,” Vanessa Cárdenas, executive director of the pro-immigration reform organization America’s Voice, told the Guardian.

The report, Economic Impacts of Trump Administration Immigration Policy, was commissioned by America’s Voice and conducted by researchers at Economic Insights and Research Consulting, a firm focused on economic analysis.

Its conclusions underscore how recent federal policies revoking immigrants’ legal protections or targeting them for enforcement have had dire effects on the nation’s affordability crisis and job market, especially in regions and industries that rely disproportionately on foreign-born workers.

In the US agricultural sector, where 42% of crop workers are undocumented and 68% are foreign-born, farmers across the country are warning that the vast majority or in some cases all of their workforce has disappeared overnight, leaving produce to fall to, or rot in, the ground and go to waste.

Food products heavily reliant on immigrant labor have experienced much sharper price increases than food overall since Trump retook the White House, according to the report.

Examples of immigrant-reliant food price increases that have exceeded the average increase in grocery prices over the last 19 months, compared with the 19 months before Trump returned to office in January 2025, are: fresh whole milk up by 5.7%, canned vegetables up by 6.3%, and apples up by 7.2%, the report found.

In that period before Trump’s inauguration, the vast majority of foods that principally depend on immigrant labor for production saw prices rise more slowly compared with other foods and some prices even fell outright, according to the report.

“One thing that changed was the [immigration] policy. Before, the trend for all those goods was a lower inflation rate. And afterward, the trend was higher inflation. So the trend was reversed, and that was quite striking,” said Robert Lynch, one of the report’s authors.

The construction industry, where foreign-born workers fill almost a third of all occupations, has also been severely affected. States more dependent on immigrant labor have seen costs for new single-family homes soar 10.9% in 2026, compared with the first eight months of 2024, bringing building projects’ monetary value from an average of $305,752 to $338,752.

And the issuance of housing permits to build single-family homes has dropped 10.6% nationwide since January 2025, with higher declines in regions more reliant on foreign-born workers, the research found.

Meanwhile, native-born Americans are missing out on potential income in hard-hit states like California, Nevada, New Jersey, Florida and New York, where construction employment is on the decline – because when there are no immigrant roofers to build a home, American electricians and plumbers lose that project, too.

“It’s not like someone can go work in construction and just not have any skills. And we’re losing people who have been here for decades working in construction. That could be fixed, but it’s going to take time,” Ettlinger said.

Other industries with soaring costs and severe labor shortages include healthcare, including home health care, nursing homes, adult daycare, lawn care, landscaping and groundskeeping, where immigrants have historically comprised a disproportionate share of the workforce and expertise.

By September 2025, less than nine months into the second Trump administration, native-born workers had already lost an estimated 51,000 to 297,000 jobs because of changes to US immigration policy, the report said. The labor force shrunk by an estimated 919,000 people during the 18 months of Trump’s second term, while job growth has slowed to roughly a third of the rate it was before he retook office.

The federal government risks losing a large segment of the $26bn in payroll taxes from unauthorized immigrants who help to support the US social security fund that pays out to American seniors – while not being able to access those benefits themselves. Now, social security trustees, including the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, labor secretary, Keith Sonderling, and social security commissioner, Frank Bisignano, are warning that lower net immigration than expected is threatening worse finances for the flailing retirement benefits system, which could mean cuts to Americans’ entitlements.

“The share of that annual loss due to the Trump immigration policy would be $2,152 [per person on average]. Thus, the Trump immigration policies, if continued, would reduce projected average annual Social Security benefits by 8.6% in 2034, and every year thereafter,” the report’s authors write.

They told the Guardian that if the administration’s immigration agenda continues as expected, the implications for the US economy could get even worse.

“We would expect higher prices,” Lynch said. “We would expect more job losses, slower economic growth and the affordability crisis getting worse – partly because prices are higher, partly because people are losing their jobs and their incomes and they can’t afford as much.”

FinanceTab.title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
FinanceTab.text:
Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets.

In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation.

The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998.

The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October.

The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated.

The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states.

Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting ​traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply.

The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to ​United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations.

Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.

Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday.

The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices.

A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall.

The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%.

The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%.

Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%.

In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

FinanceTab.title: Trump made ‘clear’ that media ban was due to critical coverage, court told
FinanceTab.text:
Donald Trump continues to be the strongest witness for the media companies arguing that they were unfairly barred from the White House at his direction, a lawyer representing CNN, MS Now and Politico told a federal judge on Thursday afternoon.

The media coalition was in court asking the judge to extend the temporary restraining order (TRO) he issued on 24 September requiring the White House to lift the ban for 14 days. That temporary reprieve was scheduled to expire on Thursday, but district court judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, said he would extend it until Tuesday and that he would probably rule on a motion for a preliminary injunction by that day. That means the White House will be forced to allow journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to continue accessing the building until at least Tuesday.

Theodore J Boutrous, who has represented numerous media companies that have sued the Trump administration over access issues, said the president made abundantly clear in a recent interview with Time magazine that he chose to bar the three news organizations because of their critical coverage of him. (Under binding court precedent, news organizations cannot be removed from the White House for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.)

Asked by Time for the “impetus” for the ban, Trump replied: “It’s just bad story after bad story, and when I say bad story, I can handle bad stories. I’ve got a lot of bad stories. Most of them are fake, and it’s not only CNN, and it’s not only MSDNC [sic]. It’s a lot of other people.” He made no mention of national security concerns, one of the primary reasons that has been given by government lawyers as a rationale for the ban.

“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge, citing what he said was “a confession of viewpoint discrimination and retaliation”. He added: “It’s really just absolutely clear … President Trump, to give him credit – he’s not hiding it.”

While the judge didn’t give a strong indication of which direction he was leaning, he accepted Boutrous’s argument when questioning the lone lawyer representing the White House, Michael Velchik.

“The decision-maker seems to have said I’m taking this action because of X and Y, and the government is saying: ‘No, it’s Z,’” the judge said. “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one around.”

Velchik, who began his argument by saying “the White House is a sacred place,” said a failure to adhere to basic standards of journalistic conduct was also one of the precipitating factors in the decision, something he said was in line with Trump’s comments criticizing the way that these three specific news organizations operate.

He also faulted the media companies for not responding to post-hoc letters giving the plaintiffs a chance to rebut the charges against them, something that Boutrous later described as a “sham process”.

In his ruling granting a TRO for the media plaintiffs, Kelly said the White House had violated constitutional requirements for due process by not giving the companies adequate notice for what the standards for acceptable conduct are and not giving them a chance to protest against the potential sanction in advance.

Nothing from Thursday’s hearing seemed to indicate that the judge had changed his thinking on that important standard, suggesting he is likely to adhere to his earlier decision-making and extend the lifting of the ban.

The judge told the government’s lawyer that they “still have a notice problem, it seems to [him], or at least a notice issue”. Kelly said the standards for adequate advance notice laid out in a binding circuit case involving a similar White House access issue “are probably the biggest hurdle you have”.

SportsTab.title: Ayra Starr on her NFL history-making half-time show
SportsTab.text:
Afrobeats singer Ayra Starr has already broken numerous records, and her NFL half-time performance this weekend is set to level up her list again.

The Nigerian star will become the first African artist to headline one of the American football league's international games when the Philadelphia Eagles take on the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on Sunday.

Ahead of the performance at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Starr told BBC Newsbeat her history-making performance "itself is a message".

Earlier this year, Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny used his Super Bowl half-time show to celebrate Latin American culture.

The 32-year-old also made history by becoming the first musician to perform entirely in Spanish at the sporting event, normally the most-watched each year on US TV.

Starr said it's "very important" for singers to seize opportunities like this.

"At the end of the day, as artists, we speak for the culture and we speak for the people that listen to us," she added.

"And we have to represent any way that seems fit, that they need."

She didn't want to give away too much about her performance, but confirmed it would feature tracks from her new studio album, Starrgirl, which was released in August.

"Sunday is gonna be amazing," she said.

"I'm still in rehearsals. It's a lot of work we're putting in so I'm really excited."

The 24-year-old has been making waves in recent years, becoming the first African woman to win best international act at the Mobo Awards and the first Nigerian woman to surpass one billion video views on YouTube.

But before she became a superstar, the singer studied for a degree in political sciences and international relations - and said this has influenced her work.

"When it comes to matters of women and equality and the girl child and even just children - I'm very outspoken on any platform that sees fit.

"Even with my music, my music is very much like 'I will do what I want' and freedom."

SportsTab.title: Trump's plans to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom
SportsTab.text:
Prices for gasoline and diesel have more than doubled since the US-Israel conflict with Iran began in February, affecting transport businesses, farmers and anyone who drives a vehicle in America.

Ahead of the critical midterm elections, there have been growing calls for more to be done to reduce the price of fuel, and US President Donald Trump has made several comments and announcements aimed at getting costs down.

With just a few weeks to go before Americans head to the polls, Trump on Friday announced a deal with President Vladimir Putin for Russian diesel to be released immediately to the US and global markets.

He said this included the immediate supply of over 300,000 tonnes, 500,000 tonnes in November and a further million tonnes "immediately thereafter".

He said this would mean diesel prices in the US and across the world "will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!".

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."

He added that a further 3m tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period" after, dependent on the condition of its refineries.

Trump's announcement of a waiver on the use of red dye diesel at a campaign stop this week underscored the importance of gas prices in a midterm election dominated by affordability issues.

The election comes as there is widespread public concern over the rising costs of fuel, food and other goods. Voters have tied the issue to Trump and his party, weighing down Republicans running in November.

Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy and the war in Iran, which has contributed to high diesel and gas prices in the US.

Global oil supplies have been restricted since the conflict in the Middle East effectively halted the usual flow of oil and refined products through the Strait of Hormuz for months.

While the flow of crude oil is nearly back to pre-war levels the price remains above $100 a barrel, and sustained high oil prices have had a knock-on effect for diesel and gasoline.

David Ruisard, pricing manager for commodities intelligence firm Argus says the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine has also impacted oil supplies, contributing to higher fuel prices.

"Our estimates are that your price increase from about $3 a gallon up to $6 a gallon [for diesel] is 60% connected to the Strait of Hormuz, 40% connected to the Russia-Ukraine conflict," he says.

Those higher energy prices are responsible for most of the uptick in inflation this year, Oxford Economics chief US economist Michael Pearce says, which is pushing up interest rates.

"The combined impact of higher rates and higher energy prices is squeezing household budgets and adding to firms' costs," he says.

While prices remain high, Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis for fuel price tracking website GasBuddy said there have been modest declines recently for both gasoline and diesel.

"A lot of that is likely due to some of the manoeuvres that we've seen the Trump administration employ over the last couple of weeks," he said.

Friday's diesel announcement is the latest in a series of policies and ideas announced by Trump.

The president announced this week that he would allow so-called red dye diesel - fuel which is used off-road and does not face federal taxes - to be used on US highways without facing federal levies.

Ruisard said the only difference in the diesel used by truck drivers and everyday consumers and the tax-free red dye diesel is the dye itself.

"The problem with that red dye is, it's extremely hard to clean it out of your tank," he explained.

The problem that creates is what happens to trucking companies that use the dyed diesel once the temporary tax relief ends, he said.

"The fines are pretty high for having that in your fuel tank because its considered tax evasion."

The other issue with expanding the use of red dye diesel, according to Ruisard, is that people and businesses - including rail operators - usually set aside a particular amount of the product.

"If suddenly people go out and they start consuming that diesel, that depletes their available supply as well," he said.

But another move from Trump has been more successful, according to analysts.

Last week, the G7 countries announced they would release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to ease supply concerns, following pressure from Trump to do so.

De Haan says the announcement itself – regardless of how much has been released so far – "has worked to push prices down to some degree".

Economist Pearce agreed but warned the release is only a temporary solution.

"As long as energy exports from the Gulf remain disrupted, stocks will need to be drained further to supply the market," he said. "And the need to refill those stocks will mean energy prices remain elevated for a period, even when disruption in the Middle East clears."

De Haan believes the president has "basically pulled all of the small levers that a president can pull, and we're still seeing prices very elevated".

"The only way out of this to reduce gas prices in a meaningful way is solve one or both of the geopolitical tensions that are causing high prices," he said.

That means reaching a deal with Iran and helping facilitate an agreement between Ukraine and Russia - which, Pearce said, are issues that cannot be directly controlled by the White House.

Even if those conflicts are resolved, Ruisard said that due to damage to facilities in the Middle East caused by military strikes it would still take production four to six months to return to normal.

"The message to consumers and industry is that regardless of what happens and whether the president is able to successfully negotiate that kind of a deal," he said.

"High prices are here to stay for a little while at least."

Additional reporting from Daniel Bush

SportsTab.title: Singapore Grand Prix: Max Verstappen beats Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton to pole
SportsTab.text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second pole position in a week by beating the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix.

Verstappen's first lap in final qualifying was enough to take pole, his time fending off a second lap from Leclerc that was 0.054 seconds off pole.

Hamilton was closest to Verstappen after the first runs but was unable to improve on his second run.

In fact, most of the front runners struggled to improve on their second runs, as Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took fourth on the grid, from McLaren's Lando Norris.

Antonelli's team-mate George Russell was sixth fastest but will drop to the back of the grid with a penalty for using too many engine parts.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was the only driver in the top four teams other than Leclerc to improve on his second run but could do no better than qualify seventh.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.

Verstappen came to Singapore fresh from his and Red Bull's first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia and he has continued where he left off.

The four-time champion has looked the man to beat all weekend, and took pole for the grand prix a few hours after winning the sprint, following Russell crashing out of the lead.

Verstappen said: "This was the one I really wanted. The car has been really strong all weekend.

"We have been on a really on a positive trend and it's really special to take the pole here."

Leclerc felt pole had been on the cards if he had not made a few small mistakes on his final lap.

He said: "Q1 and Q2 were really difficult. I had some weird struggles under braking. Q3, the lap was OK. I did some mistakes. I think there was a potential to be on pole today but Max just did a better job."

Hamilton, second to Verstappen in the sprint, was quickest in the first and second parts of qualifying but could not repeat that pace when it mattered during what he described as "another difficult Q3".

He added: "The car was feeling much better. I really felt she had more in her, pushing her through the laps and sessions. Q1 and Q2 were awesome, but got to Q3, snaps through (Turns) One and Three (on the first lap) put me down and rest of the lap was good, and then the second lap too many snaps.

"I think there's a really fine line with our car whether you are over or under the sweet spot and I didn't get it quite right today."

Hamilton said he had adjusted brake balance on his car for the final part of qualifying and he thought it had "just tipped it a little over the edge".

Antonelli's fourth place was the first relatively bright moment for the Mercedes upgrade that was introduced in Malaysia but about which the team have question marks.

Although it shows in the data to have more downforce than the previous specification, which Russell is running this weekend, it has proved difficult to access that.

In that context, for Antonelli to be only 0.189secs from pole could appear to be a promising step forward after being only seventh in sprint qualifying on Friday, even if the upgrade was still expected to deliver more performance than so far has been the case.

Russell, who crashed out of the sprint at the end of the first lap, said he had competed in qualifying "mainly just to make sure the car was feeling as it did yesterday after the crash but it didn't quite feel the same".

He added: "I had great pace yesterday. We were in the top three every lap I completed. And today I wasn't in the top five at any point throughout the session so we need to understand why that is."

McLaren had hoped for a step forward this weekend after struggling in the past two races but fifth and seventh marked only a small amount of progress for the world champions, despite flashes of promise through the weekend.

Norris said: "In the end we're where we should be. Nothing has changed so no reason why we would suddenly be on the pace. I could put good bits together, but the car is just too much of a challenge, I have to feel like I am almost crashing to put in a purple sector but you just can't do that, the tyres don't survive, the car is too difficult to be in that perfect limit when it's quick."

Norris addressed the incident with Piastri on the final lap of the sprint race, when an attack by the Briton into Turn Five led to them colliding, and turning what had been fourth and fifth places into an eighth for Norris and retirement for Piastri.

Norris said: "There are two sides. One is what the stewards say and that's a fair reasoning, no-one's to blame.

"But I did apologise because it was still me attacking, as I had the right to do. If I just sat there and was boring like I should be, nothing would have happened. So really it's still my fault but I deserved to go for the space and I still believe I had the right for it."

SportsTab.title: Arsenal 2-1 Leeds: A decisive moment of real quality - but Mikel Arteta still has issues to address
SportsTab.text:
For the second time in three Premier League matches, Bruno Guimaraes has come to Arsenal's rescue.

Having sparked their 2-0 win at Sunderland in September with the crucial first goal, the £75m summer signing came off the bench again to have a pivotal impact against Leeds on Saturday.

This time it was the winner as the Gunners came from behind for a 2-1 success in a testing encounter at Emirates Stadium.

But Ecuador international Piero Hincapie was carried off during the warm-down, raising concern the defender has suffered an injury.

He came on as a late substitute against Daniel Farke's side but completed extra running after the final whistle - a practice most clubs use.

A fifth win in six league games put Mikel Arteta's side level on points with leaders Manchester City, but their title defence has certainly not been without its scares so far.

Following on from their comprehensive 3-0 defeat at Brighton last time out, Arsenal fell behind in a league match for a third time in four league matches - and only a David Raya penalty save stopped them from trailing at Sunderland as well.

For large parts of the game against Leeds, they were nowhere near their best but, after going behind in the 55th minute, Riccardo Calafiori and Guimaraes - on his full home debut - secured an important three points.

"It was a great game of football. Leeds were brilliant for one hour." said Ally McCoist on TNT Sports.

"Mikel Arteta made changes when he needed to and the substitutions gave Arsenal what they needed. That's what champions do. Leeds can hold their heads high."

By getting wins when below par the mark of champions or are there reasons for concern for Arteta and Arsenal?

Coming into the season as defending champions, Arsenal were looking to make a statement signing to make their rivals take notice.

They did not bring in the attacker they wanted but Guimaraes looks like he could be that key arrival to help Arteta's men build on their success.

The 28-year-old midfielder is a 'win-now' signing in the peak years of his career.

He responded well to a disappointing performance in the defeat by Brighton, where he made his full league debut.

The Brazilian international has now scored two goals that have helped his side to valuable points and justified the decision to spend big on Guimaraes, even if the Gunners are inundated with top quality options in midfield.

Arteta said: "He wasn't at that level against Brighton, and this is the level for Arsenal. Every week, every game, every minute, every action, you have to be at that level.

"Today was much better. That's what we have to demand, and this is what I demand to myself. I'm going to demand the same with the players, because if we do that, he will raise the standards and we will be a better team."

Guimaraes was the first player to score twice from the bench this season and both goals have been from outside the box.

Arsenal won the league last season in part because of their excellent defence.

The Gunners conceded the fewest goals in the league but have already conceded five in six games.

The partnership of Gabriel Magalhaes and William Saliba is one of the best in the world and Arsenal look to be missing the injured Frenchman's calmness.

Ezri Konsa was brought in from Aston Villa for £55m and, despite his quality, is still getting used to his new surroundings.

It is unclear how serious Hincapie's injury is, although he was seen clutching his right ankle as he was carried off by goalkeeper Illan Meslier.

He signed for the club on a permanent deal this summer, having initially joined on loan from Bayer Leverkusen last season.

Hincapie has suffered from muscular issues this term and now faces an anxious wait to discover whether he requires another spell on the sidelines.

Left-back Calafiori, though, has proved integral to Arsenal's attacking threat. His equaliser against Leeds was his first league strike this term but no defender has been involved in more Premier League goals than the Italian (one goal, two assists).

"The last time we put our shirts on, something was missing." added Arteta.

"And we need to be very conscious of that. From being exceptional and being the champions to being extremely average, like in that game, is a really thin line.

"So if you don't want it more than the opponent, you are not able to cope emotionally with certain situations, you're going to suffer.

"And we all suffered and we didn't enjoy that game, but then you have to learn the lesson and we certainly done that.

"We speak about it and you could sense that there was something in those tummies."

Arteta made some big calls when naming his starting XI.

He opted to start with German Kai Havertz up front despite the forward returning early from international duty after picking up a hamstring issue, leaving Viktor Gyokeres on the bench again.

Gyokeres had scored four goals, registering in every match for Sweden, in the last international break, but looks to have work to do to win his manager round.

The 28-year-old has yet to start a Premier League game and in his cameos this season has looked far from the level required as a striker who could fire Arsenal to back-to-back titles.

The forward line did not click against Leeds and, with Havertz looking like he lacked match sharpness, thoughts turned towards whether Arsenal missing out on an elite attacker in the summer would haunt them.

Winger Christos Tzolis, who has shone at times this season following his summer arrival, suffered a hamstring issue with Greece and, with Eberechi Eze out of form, Arteta used Noni Madueke on the left wing.

Madueke was left out of the last England squad due to a lack of minutes with Arsenal but, after "being the best player in training for the last 10 days" according to Arteta, now could be the chance for him to prove his worth.

SportsTab.title: The Prem: Northampton 71-48 Bath: Saints score 11 tries to beat Bath in try-fest
SportsTab.text:
Northampton (26) 71

Tries: F Smith, Sleightholme 3, Freeman 2, Dingwall, Pater, Kemeny, Mitchell, Coles Cons: F Smith 8

Tries: Carr-Smith, C Griffin, A Griffin, Green 2, Carreras, Bayliss Cons: Russell 5 Pens: Russell

Northampton came out on top of a high-octane 18-try thriller at home to Bath, the second highest scoring game in English top-flight history.

The two sides had surpassed 100 points on the scoreboard with 15 minutes remaining and continued to showcase unstoppable, attacking flair as the play went end-to-end.

Northampton eventually streaked clear in the second half, with Ollie Sleightholme scoring a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman scoring twice as they finished with 11 tries and bounced back from defeat by Bristol a week ago.

The loss is the first of the season for Bath, who made 12 changes for the match, with Arthur Green getting two of their seven tries and Charlie Griffin also scoring one on his Prem debut.

The 119 points scored falls short of the record in the English top flight - the 127 points shared in Saints' 94-33 win over Bristol in May.

Rory Hutchinson fed Fin Smith to cross first for Saints and while Bath arrived with a younger-looking starting XV there was no evidence of inexperience, as a moment of world-class Finn Russell skill opened a gap for Green to break through and Tom Carr-Smith to cross.

Bath hit Northampton again through 21-year-old Charlie Griffin before Saints slickly whipped the ball between their backs until it reached Sleightholme for their second try.

Tommy Freeman dived under the posts for Northampton's third right after Bath's Josh Bayliss was shown yellow for repeated infringements but, again, there was nothing to separate the sides as Archie Griffin rolled over under two tacklers for the visitors' third.

Kepu Tuipulotu barged through midfield and found Green to make it 26-19 to Bath, which was quickly cancelled out by Fraser Dingwall's score at the other end, leaving Russell's penalty on the stroke of half-time the only mark of difference.

SportsTab.title: Australia vs South Africa: Matt Renshaw epic innings puts tourists in command
SportsTab.text:
First Test, Durban (day two of five)

Australia 390: Renshaw 190, Cummins 43; Mulder 4-68

South Africa 27-1: Markram 15*: Hazlewood 1-9

Matt Renshaw scored an epic first Test century in more than nine years to put Australia in control of the first Test in their highly anticipated series against South Africa.

After much talk about the issues among their ageing top order on day one, Renshaw ground out a majestic career-best 190 from 397 balls in Durban, emphatically pushing his case to be part of Australia's future.

The 30-year-old was born in Middlesbrough and was a childhood friend of England captain Joe Root - their fathers played together in English club cricket - before his parents left the UK for New Zealand and then Australia when he was seven.

As well as potentially match-defining innings, having dragged Australia from 124-6 to 390 all out, it was a statement knock from Renshaw who has had an in-out international career.

"I like him as a player," former Australia batter Simon Katich said on SEN Radio.

"When he first came in, I liked him as a player, even though others thought he was too defensive.

"I think that is what this team has needed and been crying out for."

Renshaw scored 184 in his fourth Test against Pakistan in January 2017 after being handed a debut aged 20, but averaged 19.41 across 10 Tests across two spells before being recalled earlier this year.

"A few years out of the team, I had the opportunity in 2023, you think [you're] never going to get the opportunity again," Renshaw said.

"When I hit the ball [to go to his hundred] I was screaming at it 'go, go, go'.

"It hit me all at once. It was pretty special."

Against South Africa, the left-hander hit only three boundaries on day one - he attacked only 14.2% of deliveries in making his first 50 runs, the lowest figure of the Australia's top order. A throwback innings continued as he left well throughout day two, largely scoring square or behind the wicket.

He extended his partnership with captain Pat Cummins in the morning session to 86 and then expertly controlled a stand of 134 with number 10 Nathan Lyon to frustrate and tire South Africa's bowlers.

Renshaw took the strike when needed, protecting Lyon from the pace of Anrich Nortje, but became increasingly aggressive to add boundaries and inflict further pain as the partnership grew.

He added a further 21 alongside number 11 Josh Hazlewood before falling in the first over after tea.

Renshaw's superb innings, and opener Ryan Rickelton's three-ball duck in the 8.4 overs before bad light halted South Africa's reply, has left Australia well placed to push for victory on a pitch that flattened out on day two, but is expected to take turn later in the Test.

This series has been eagerly anticipated, given it is a repeat of last year's World Test Championship final, which was won by the Proteas.

It is also the third in a possible 21 Tests for Australia before the end of the Ashes next summer and, while Renshaw has surely secured his immediate future at least, his knock does not alleviate all questions over the make-up of their side.

When he was recalled in August it was in place of Jake Weatherald as opener, but he was moved down to number five for this Test when Cameron Green was ruled out.

Nic Maddinson came in at the top of the order alongside Travis Head, giving Australia an 11th different opening partnership since the retirement of David Warner.

With Green, the regular number five, expected to return and Maddinson making a 33-ball duck on day one, a solution to their top-order struggles would be to move Renshaw up again.

That would reunite him with Head, who made the surprise move to opener to impressive effect in the Ashes - he flogged England for centuries in Perth, Adelaide and Sydney - but has also shown vulnerability in failing to pass 22 in his four innings since.

Equally, Renshaw could stay in the middle order and Green return for fellow-all-rounder Beau Webster, meaning Australia's hunt for a settled opening pair would continue.

"No idea," Renshaw said of the decision ahead. "That's well above my pay grade.

"Whatever is the best for the team is the one for me. I am not too fussed."

SportsTab.title: Singapore Grand Prix: Max Verstappen wins sprint from Lewis Hamilton after George Russell crashes out
SportsTab.text:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won an incident-packed sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix after Mercedes driver George Russell crashed out of the lead.

Russell was leading in tricky conditions, with half the track dry and half wet, when he got a little too wide at the final corner at the end of the first lap.

He lost control of his Mercedes, which spun across the track into the inside wall, before bouncing back again to the outside, the rest of the field somehow avoiding him.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton took second having made a superb start from sixth on the grid with team-mate Charles Leclerc third.

A final-lap collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri at Turn Five promoted Russell's team-mate Kimi Antonelli to fourth place.

In combination with Russell's retirement, that extends the Italian's championship lead to 89 points.

A chaotic race saw the start delayed by 30 minutes by a tropical downpour, and then Verstappen navigating a safety car period following Russell's accident, a restart, and initial pressure from Hamilton to eventually ease away into a comfortable lead.

It was the Dutchman's second Formula 1 win in seven days, after his maiden victory this season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and the first time he has won in Singapore.

The rain before the start hit only parts of the track. The second sector stayed dry while the first sector, particularly Turns Two and Three, were soaking wet with standing water.

Once the rain abated, the field did two laps behind a safety car to check conditions before racing began with a standing start.

Russell gave himself a golden opportunity to breathe some life into his almost-extinguished title hopes when he beat Verstappen off the line and took the lead into the first corner.

But after leading the first lap, he made a mistake at the final corner.

Russell said: "I just misjudged it, got more power than I was expecting from the battery, got a little wider than I expected and touched the white line. Rule number one in the wet is don't touch the white line. Very silly mistake."

That left Verstappen in front, with Hamilton behind. But after the seven-time champion pursued his erstwhile 2021 title rival for a few laps, the Red Bull began to ease away and was clearly in control, leading Hamilton, Leclerc, Piastri, Norris and Antonelli.

With overtaking difficult around Marina Bay, the field was static until the closing stages.

Leclerc was struggling, and he began to be caught by the McLarens and Antonelli.

Norris had been pressuring Piastri for some laps before the Australian also began to close in on Leclerc, and Antonelli, struggling with oversteer in the early laps, picked up the pace.

On the final lap, Norris made a better exit out of Turn Three and saw an opportunity to try to pass Piastri at Turn Five, but Piastri defended his position robustly, the cars touched, and spun in unison.

Norris was initially far enough alongside to make a legitimate passing attempt, but having apparently tried to back out of the move, not so at the apex to satisfy the driving standards rules.

But the criticism of Norris will be that he miscalculated the risk-reward, that it was an ill-advised, marginal move against his team-mate for little gain - a point was at stake - and none for the team, as it would have not changed their collective points total.

The stewards investigated the incident but took no action on the basis that both drivers had contributed to the incident.

Piastri, who hit the barriers, was out on the spot, but Norris was able to keep going, although he fell down to eighth, behind Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson, Haas driver Oliver Bearman and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg.

SportsTab.title: Arsenal v Leeds : How the players rated
SportsTab.text:
Arsenal came from behind as the champions beat Leeds United 2-1 at Emirates Stadium.

James Justin scored the opener for Leeds before Riccardo Calafiori levelled with Bruno Guimaraes coming off the bench to score the winner.

Here's how I rated the players and you can see how you scored them below.

David Raya: A smart save to stop Jayden Bogle and then an even better one to deny Gudmundsson soon after. The cross for the Leeds goal evaded him though. 6

Ben White: His header set-up Calafiori for the equaliser. Caught offside a couple of times when Arsenal were building good attacks in the first half. The Leeds goal came down his side. 6

Ezri Konsa: Involved with the physical battle against Calvert-Lewin. 6

Gabriel Magalhaes: It was not the usual convincing performance from the Arsenal back four or Gabriel. 6

Riccardo Calafiori: Scored the equaliser after Arsenal went behind. Tried to make things happen with his adventurous runs but the Arsenal attack did not click. 7

Declan Rice: Tried to inject some energy into the Arsenal as they struggled to create in the first half. A clever assist for Bruno Guimaraes winner. 7

Myles Lewis-Skelly: Back in the Arsenal starting line-up after being dropped for Bruno Guimaraes. Not his best day. 6

Martin Odegaard: Tried to get on the ball to make things happen and had a tame effort saved by Trafford. 6

Bukayo Saka: The winger caused Gudmundsson some problems early but never capitalised on the opportunities. Missed a big late chance to add a third. 6

Noni Madueke: Given the chance to start on the left wing in place of the injured Christos Tzolis. Some good deliveries but not enough of a threat throughout the game. 6

Kai Havertz: Included from the start after picking up a hamstring injury on international duty. Did not look at full match sharpness. 6

Viktor Gyokeres (on 63, Havertz): Brought physicality to the attack. 6

Bruno Guimaraes (on 63, Lewis-Skelly): Came on, changed the game and scored the winner. 8

Jurrien Timber (on 63, White): A calming presence in the backline. 7

Piero Hincapie (on 82, Calafiori): Brought on to see out the win. 6

Merino (on 90, Odegaard): No time to impact. 5

Subs not used: Arrizabalaga, Zubimendi, Eze, Dowman.

SportsTab.title: Giro di Lombardia: Rider safety protest delays start of UCI World Tour race won by 20-year-old Paul Seixas
SportsTab.text:
Riders at the Giro di Lombardia staged a protest which delayed the start of the race by five minutes as they sought to draw attention to safety concerns following a series of incidents.

Organisers completed the countdown and a starting flag was waved but the peloton remained stationary, creating confusion among spectators in Bergamo, Italy.

Belgium's Remco Evenepoel then addressed the crowd, saying "there are too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race" and highlighting the death of British cyclist Fin Tarling, who died in a collision with a vehicle at the Volta a Portugal in August.

"Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and a colleague, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do," added double Olympic champion Evenepoel.

After five minutes had elapsed, a second starting flag was waved and the riders set off for Como.

French 20-year-old Paul Seixas broke with 19km to go to become the youngest winner of the Giro di Lombardia and the youngest winner of a Monument race since 1944.

Seixas finished 48 seconds ahead of Spain's Enric Mas, having dropped Italy's Giulio Ciccone and Great Britain's Tom Pidcock, who finished third and sixth respectively, shortly after his break.

His solo ride for over 18km saw him take a Monument title in only his third appearance, having made his debut with a seventh-place finish in this race last year.

"This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses," said the CPA union, which represents professional cyclists, in a statement which was re-posted on Instagram by riders including Evenepoel and Pidcock., external

"This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer."

The CPA has called for cycling's governing body, the UCI, to help ensure race organisers "take responsibility" and "act" to improve safety standards.

Earlier this week, Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubi were struck by a police motorcycle travelling in the opposite direction during the Tre Valli Varesine race.

"Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met," the CPA statement added.

"We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one.

"We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."

The Giro di Lombardia is the last of the season's five Monuments, a set of long-standing, prestigious one-day races.

It has been won by Tadej Pogacar for the past five years but the Slovenian was not present at the race, which is also the penultimate event on this year's UCI World Tour calendar, after sustaining a season-ending injury at the Vuelta a Espana.

Seixas, who finished fourth in this year's Tour de France, also finished second behind Pogacar at Liege–Bastogne–Liege, his only other Monument appearance this season.

The Decathlon–CMA CGM rider is the first Frenchman to win a Monument since Julian Alaphilippe at Milan–San Remo in 2019, and the first to triumph at the Giro di Lombardia since Thibaut Pinot in 2018.

SportsTab.title: Edinburgh top URC after bonus-point win over Zebre
SportsTab.text:
United Rugby Championship

Tries: Fusco, Ferrari Cons: Allan

Tries: M. Currie, Douglas, Bradbury, T. Currie Cons: Grayson 3 Pens: Grayson

Edinburgh went top of the nascent United Rugby Championship table as a bonus-point victory at Zebre made it three wins from three for Sean Everitt's injury-hit side.

James Grayson kicked a penalty to put the visitors in front early on, but after winger Malelili Satala was sin-binned for a deliberate knock-on, Italy scrum-half Alessandro Fusco put Zebre in front with the game's first try.

Edinburgh recovered from that setback though and retook the lead on the half-hour mark when centre Matt Currie crashed through a couple of Zebre defenders to dot down.

From that moment, Edinburgh never ceded control.

With half-time approaching, Fusco was yellow carded and from the subsequent attack, young flanker Freddy Douglas scored at the back of an Edinburgh maul.

The game followed a similar pattern after the break, with the Scottish outfit dominating both possession and territory.

Magnus Bradbury powered over under the posts for Edinburgh's third try and although Zebre's Giacamo Ferrari narrowed the deficit after Edinburgh's replacement hooker Harri Morris was yellow carded, the hosts never threatened to turn things around.

And in the final minute of the contest, another powerful maul allowed Tom Currie to score Edinburgh's fourth try and ensure they would take maximum points.

SportsTab.title: Greek takeaways: What did we learn from England's World Cup play-off win in Crete?
SportsTab.text:
England came away from Greece with a valuable first-leg lead in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off - but what did we learn?

Sarina Wiegman's side are looking to secure their place in Brazil next year but have to navigate the play-offs after finishing runners-up in their qualification group.

The back-to-back European champions won 3-1 in Crete on Friday night and will need to finish the job against Greece on Tuesday in Leicester (19:30 BST).

The winner of the tie faces Ukraine or Slovakia in round two to decide who will head to Brazil.

Lucy Bronze withdrew from the squad with a minor injury earlier this week, handing a rare opportunity to Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier.

The defender is a key player for her club but struggles to break into the England team with Bronze understandably a tough figure to displace.

Wiegman sees Le Tissier as a right-back as opposed to a centre-back - which is her position at United - and that meant she was handed a start against Greece.

Making her 15th cap, Le Tissier was a standout performer and was rewarded with her first international goal in the 63rd minute, providing optimism for a future without 34-year-old Bronze.

"As soon as we were in possession, she was higher on the pitch and she already came close to a couple of moments with crosses," said Wiegman.

"I'm very happy for her and for the whole team because that was an important goal."

It was just England's third win in their past eight competitive away games.

A 3-1 victory is a pleasing result, but given the gulf in class, Wiegman admitted frustrations at not keeping a clean sheet.

There were familiar lapses in concentration defensively that gave Greece opportunities to pounce. Ioanna Papatheodorou struck the crossbar in the first half, before teeing up Kallisti Brouksair for their goal later on.

Those chances came from England errors and the lack of clean sheet means the door remains open for Greece in the second leg.

"That's up to us. We have to show up on Tuesday, play a good game and then we should be better than Greece," said Wiegman.

"Of course we want to take some more distance [in the scoreline], that's absolutely true, but at the same time we won and that's the most important thing.

"Sometimes we played really well and sometimes we were a bit sloppy. We were a bit frustrated as we wanted to do that better.

"We want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too."

With victory secure, Wiegman was able to hand a debut to 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson, as well as Liverpool captain Grace Fisk.

Fisk, 28, had waited more than six years for her debut, having received her first England call-up in 2020 but Parkinson has broken through at pace this season.

The teenager was unexpectedly named in Wiegman's squad in March, having only made the jump up to England's Under-23s a few months earlier.

She secured a move to the United States this summer, joining North Carolina Courage from Portuguese side Valadares Gaia, and came on in the 85th minute.

This week defender Esme Morgan said: "She's a really intelligent player. She has incredibly good movement and timing, picking up pockets for players to find her.

"She's really comfortable receiving [the ball] in tight spaces, she's strong holding off players, very aggressive in her tackling and wins back a lot of balls.

"I've been really impressed with Erica since she came into camp and also from playing against her in the National Women's Soccer League."

Parkinson's debut added to the debate of who Wiegman's preferred number 10 is.

She is one of many options available, including Chelsea forward Lauren James, who was given a creative, free role against Greece.

James showed flashes of quality and nonchalantly lobbed goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti from 30 yards in the first half, but her effort was ruled out for offside.

Other options include Manchester City's Grace Clinton and Manchester United's Ella Toone, who were both recalled to the squad to cover injuries with Aston Villa's Lucia Kendall among those to drop out.

Laura Blindkilde Brown started in that position with James in Crete, while Beth Mead and Jess Park have also played there before.

The position was a difficult one for Wiegman to nail down at Euro 2025 and more than a year later, the question of who is England's best number 10 remains.

"I see there is a lot of competition in that position, where we have a lot of options with different players, who have different qualities," said Wiegman.

"You can call it a question mark but I call it many options. Today we had two 10s and sometimes three. [James] was one of them."

Local media had questioned why the game wasn't being played in Greece's capital city Athens.

And there was an eerie atmosphere with fewer than 4,000 fans in the 26,000-capacity stadium in Heraklion, Crete.

The Lionesses are also not used to being in play-offs, a route they are having to take after finishing runners-up to world champions Spain in their qualifying group.

But Georgia Stanway, this year's top scorer for England, once again turned up when they needed her to and she opened the scoring after a neat, incisive passing move, in a frustrating first half.

That was the spark England needed as they lacked ruthlessness and failed to capitalise on their dominance - an aspect of their game that needs improving.

"I think we made it a bit harder. Greece were well prepared and disciplined. We struggled when they tried to press us," added Wiegman.

"We could have scored more than the three goals. There are lots of things to take. I have seen some fluid moments but I want more.

"The final ball, final cross and the positions can be better. Of course, we are working on that. We have an opportunity to improve that on Tuesday."

SportsTab.title: Manchester United v Tottenham: Premier League – live
SportsTab.text:
32 min: Tielemans obstructs Gallagher as the Spurs man cuts in from the left. A free kick and a chance to load the box …

30 min: United finally put some pressure on the Spurs defence, Shaw making a nuisance of himself down the left, the visitors unable to clear as a game of head tennis breaks out. Eventually the flag goes up for offside, but that’s better from the hosts. “Is it somewhere in recently enacted legislation that United have to start matches poorly, looking utterly confused at all times by opponent’s desire to score?” wonders David Cahill.

28 min: Gray saunters out of the Spurs defence in the manner of peak-era Beckenbauer. However peak-era Beckenbauer usually had challenges to evade. United make none, until Mbeumo eventually fouls him, putting an end to a 35-yard sashay. More groans.

26 min: Lammens hoicks another pass out of play, and has some choice words for his defenders. He didn’t want that latest passback. Eff! Jeff! Discord!

25 min: … Fernandes plays the free kick short, to more rumbles of concern, before eventually sending in a cross that’s easily cleared. The home fans on the edge of full revolt. United have been dreadful.

24 min: Bergvall tugs at Cuhna’s shirt and is fortunate not to go into the book. Just a free kick out on the left. United load the Spurs box and …

23 min: On the touchline, Roberto De Zerbi holds his head in his hands. He can’t believe that silky move didn’t end in a goal. He surely won’t believe his team aren’t in front. Michael Carrick meanwhile looks calm, if concerned. The mood in the home crowd is beginning to curdle … and there are some loud boos as Lammens shanks a clearance out of play for a throw.

21 min: Udogie and Savio combine crisply down the left. The ball’s cut back for Kudus, who spins and whistles a low drive inches wide of the bottom left. No idea how Spurs aren’t leading this match; they’ve been absurdly dominant.

20 min: Mbeumo crosses from the left. Diallo slides in but can’t force the ball past a combination of Udogie and Kinsky. That’s better from United, though their bar is set so low right now.

19 min: Maguire tries to usher the ball out for a goal kick. Solanke manages to hook a leg around him and instigate a game of bagatelle in the six-yard box. Maguire and United get away with it as the ball pings clear of the danger zone.

17 min: Bergvall is given a preposterous amount of time in a pocket of space in front of the United D. Fernandes not tracking back, the defence not closing down. Bergvall aims for the top-right corner but gets it all wrong. Goal kick, but United are really pushing their luck here. They need to get a grip of midfield and quick. Spurs have been excellent and are well on top.

15 min: Gallagher steals the ball off the snoozing Maguire’s toe near the centre circle. He feeds Savio down the left. Yoro ushers player and ball out for a goal kick. Yoro’s started really impressively; that’s just as well for United, because without those last two interventions, Spurs could easily have snaffled a couple of goals.

14 min: Bergvall nearly latches onto a loose ball just inside the United box on the left. He’s blocked by a sensational sliding tackle from Yoro. Full marks, but that had to be timed perfectly, and United’s defence is operating right on the edge at the moment.

12 min: Kudus looks electric. He skins Cunha down the right and makes towards the box along the byline. Cunha sticks an arm on his shoulder and lightly tugs. If Kudus goes down, the ref has a decision to make. But he stays on his feet and cuts back to nobody. Cunha treading a fine line there.

Updated at 13.02 EDT

10 min: Kudus and Bergvall combine down the right, the latter’s cross blocked and deflected back to Lammens. Savio then nicks the ball of a dawdling Tielemans, but the whistle goes as he advances on the United box. There was contact, but not very much, and that’s a generous award of a foul to get Tielemans out of trouble.

8 min: Lammens hesitates with the ball at his feet – admittedly having taken possession of an unwanted backpass from Martinez – and is nearly closed down. He clears just in time. Already a few concerned mutters from the home fans, who regroup and try to chant their heroes into waking up. Nearly 40 percent of this match has been played in United’s final third.

Updated at 12.41 EDT

7 min: Kudus dribbles down the right and is brought to a halt by a combination of Mainoo and Shaw. Nothing comes of the free kick, but Spurs come again through Kudus, who spins into space down the right and crosses for Solanke, who can’t win a header six yards out. United clear their lines, but it’s all Spurs in these opening exchanges.

Updated at 13.00 EDT

6 min: Udogie has a chance to feed Solanke down the inside-left channel, but hesitates and the open channel is quickly closed. Spurs have started brightly. “If ever there was a good time to play Tottenham at home it’s now,” begins Dave Estherby. “Stone dead last and can’t buy a goal. However, Utd’s defence has been worryingly porous all season (whadda ya mean it’s only game six?!) and after struggling to hit the proverbial barn door at Fulham Carrick’s bum may be a tad squeaky at the prospect of this one. Not that he should worry too much - if he gets sacked before Xmas he can simply come back as interim in January, that’ll work.”

4 min: … and now Gallagher is booked for a needless tug on Maguire in midfield. He’s got a lot of time left to tread on eggshells.

3 min: Spurs should be leading. Lammens plays a dreadful pass out from the box. It’s intercepted by Bergvall, who feeds Solanke, one on one with the keeper! He should slot into the bottom right, but clanks his shot straight at the stopper, who sticks out a strong arm to make up for his mistake. What a chance.

Updated at 12.56 EDT

2 min: Mbeumo spins Van Hecke and is clipped by Bergvall in the centre circle. Any later in the match and it could have been a booking. Should, maybe? It isn’t, though. Cunha tries to take a quick free kick but the referee whistles to put a stop to the caper. And that’s the end of all that.

Spurs get the ball rolling. They’re kicking towards the Stretford End in this first half.

The teams are out. Manchester United in their famous red, white and black, Tottenham in second-choice dark blue with diagonal multi-coloured neon nonsense. Meanwhile here’s the first line of a song ringing out loud from all four corners of Old Trafford: “You know what you are.” No prizes for guessing the rest of the lyrics, or which club they’re serenading. Don’t look back in anger? Good luck with that! We’ll be off in a minute.

Updated at 12.37 EDT

Tottenham coach Roberto De Zerbi’s turn to talk to Sky. “[Micky van de Ven does not start] because he plays four games in a row for 90 minutes … we have a squad good enough to change … Marcos Senesi is one of the first XI players no less than Micky or any other centre-back … when Lucas [Bergvall] has played this season he has done very well … [Sandro] Tonali did not play the last international game so I think he is fresh to play … both give quality.”

Manchester United coach Michael Carrick speaks to Sky Sports. “We’re obviously delighted [Amad Diallo is back] … he’s a big part of the group … he offers us an awful lot … it’s nice to have him back … he was looking really good pre-season … he’s close to being back to his best … [Leny Yoro] is at the stage of his career to make the next step … he’s made his debut for France … fully deserved … we look forward to seeing him play … we want to keep moving forward … keep improving … we’ve added a little bit … we’ve had to clean up and sharpen up a few other things … get the balance right … today’s a good time to start.”

The results of the 3pms are in. In the main, it’s been a good afternoon for bottom-placed Spurs: Fulham, Bournemouth and Sunderland all lost, while Aston Villa failed to win, so should Roberto De Zerbi’s men claim all three points this evening, they could catapult up the table as high (realistically) as 14th. Ipswich’s late comeback at Fulham however means Manchester United can only climb as high as 10th with victory here. Sarah Rendell has all the details in today’s Clockwatch.

Aston Villa 2-2 Brentford

Chelsea 5-1 Bournemouth

Ipswich Town 2-1 Fulham

Sunderland 0-2 Brighton & Hove Albion

Updated at 12.18 EDT

This is, of course, a rerun of the 2025 Europa League final. (Bilbao’s a lovely city, though the puppy outside the Guggenheim is a bit underwhelming.) History also offers us all of this …

…. plus one of the great training-ground free-kick routines, right at the very start of this old-school classic. Another six-goal thriller, please, lads!

Amad Diallo isn’t alone in making his first appearance for a while. Also starring at Old Trafford this afternoon, this City-baiting banner beloved of United fans back in the day …

… now updated for the post-guilty-verdict era. Opinions / interpretations / blood-pressure readings may vary, many of which can be sourced elsewhere on your super soaraway internet.

Manchester United make two changes to their starting XI following the 1-1 draw at Fulham three years weeks ago. Leny Yoro and Amad Diallo are in for Diogo Dalot and Marcus Rashford, who both drop to the bench. Diallo is making his first appearance of the season. Still no sign of Matthijs de Ligt.

Tottenham Hotspur switch out over half their team in the sepia-toned wake of the dim-and-distant 2-3 home defeat to Aston Villa. Archie Gray, Lucas Bergvall, Destiny Udogie, Conor Gallagher, Marcos Senesi and Mohammed Kudus are recalled. Omar Marmoush, Mateus Fernandes, Rodrigo Bentancur and captain Micky van de Ven drop to the bench, while Pedro Porro and Andy Robertson are missing through injury.

Updated at 12.18 EDT

Manchester United: Lammens, Yoro, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw, Tielemans, Mainoo, Diallo, Fernandes, Mbeumo, Cunha.

Subs: Darlow, Dalot, Mount, Rashford, Zirkzee, Santos, Baleba, Heaven, Lacey.

Tottenham Hotspur: Kinsky, Gray, van Hecke, Senesi, Udogie, Bergvall, Tonali, Savio, Gallagher, Kudus, Solanke.

Subs: Dubravka, Adarabioyo, Maddison, Tel, Fernandes, Marmoush, Bentancur, Davies, van de Ven.

Referee: Stuart Attwell

VAR: Jarred Gillett

Updated at 11.44 EDT

Two teams here who had some forward momentum going into the season with genuine hope of picking up speed; two teams who stalled on the starting line as the leading riders whistled off into the distance. Now then, it’s way too early to be bandying about talk of crisis … but Tottenham Hotspur are bottom of the table after being schooled at home by Aston Villa, while Manchester United required a late equaliser at no-win Fulham to ensure the three-week international hiatus wasn’t as much as a drag for their fans as it would have been without that verdict. Problem is, another unsatisfactory result isn’t going to help the off-stage mood music for any of these lads. So this is important. On offer tonight: a big momentum-shifter for both sides. Throw in the fact that this is one of the glamour fixtures in English football, and a cold start to the campaign can’t compromise the genuine sizzle when these two get together. The spark is lit at 5.30pm BST. It’s on!

TechnologyTab.title: Palantir AI probe leads to Met Police volunteer chief's dismissal
TechnologyTab.text:
The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.

The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.

Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.

The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.

He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.

Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.

"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software.

The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems.

In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.

He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers.

The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations.

Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure.

Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration.

Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir.

Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company, warned against "mob rule" in government procurement.

Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?'

"Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."

TechnologyTab.title: King Charles warns malicious online actors are evolving their tactics
TechnologyTab.text:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.
