EntertainmentTab.title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
EntertainmentTab.text:
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.

The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.

Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.

The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.

Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.

Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".

"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.

"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."

He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Jelliness is my life motto’: jackpot theatre prize winner Jaha Koo on kimchi, K-pop and his robotic eel
EntertainmentTab.text:
When I meet Jaha Koo in Oslo, where he has just been honoured with the prestigious International Ibsen award, I hand him a congratulatory packet of Haribo. The alternative would be a jar of kimchi but one of the many things you learn from Koo’s captivating theatre shows is that air travel and fermented vegetables can be a disastrous combo. When he moved to Berlin from South Korea with 10kg of his grandma’s finest kimchi, it became “bloated like a dead whale” and exploded on his balcony. His new neighbours were unimpressed.

In Koo’s current touring production, Haribo Kimchi, he examines how this unlikely fusion of two foods represents his cultural identity. He does so while preparing an onstage banquet for two lucky audience members. Despite spending many years in Europe, where Haribo gummies originated around a century ago, Koo still finds himself considered foremost as Korean by Europeans. But when he returns to his original homeland he is not always seen as Korean either.

We meet the day after the ceremony for the Ibsen award, founded by the Norwegian government and rewarding the winner with a huge 2.5m kroner (£200,000). Its past recipients include Lola Arias, Taylor Mac and Forced Entertainment. Koo cheerfully packs away my sweets for the next day’s flight to Belgium, where he is now based, and outlines his life motto of “jelliness”. It was only when he arrived in Europe that he started to eat gummy bears. “When you push jelly, it can shrink and change form but after a few seconds, it recovers its shape,” he says. “That is the same resilience I need to improve when I live outside Korea.” In the show, he explains how the bears’ smiley faces cheer him up when he’s feeling down.

If Haribo was a new discovery, kimchi “was there before I was born and it was waiting for me”. As a Korean, he says, it is impossible to think about food without this quintessential side dish and he is part of “a kimchi diaspora”. The exact ingredients may differ around the world, depending on what’s available, but that doesn’t make any recipe inauthentic, he says: “Kimchi can be very diverse.” When he prepares the dish in Belgium, it sums up how he is true to his roots yet adapting to a new environment – “a kind of cultural assimilation”.

Koo is an artist adept at setting out his stall – literally so in the case of Haribo Kimchi, where the set is a Korean snack cart called a pojangmacha. It’s a movable feast, typically frequented by hungry customers of all backgrounds and generations – “kind of like a soul place,” he says. “They want to find comfort, eat quite humble food.” The roof of Koo’s bar has a Haribo-red glow that is translucent – a signifier, he suggests, of in-between states, much as the pojangmachas suggest lives in transit. “They are movable. There is no address. They appear in the evening and then disappear.” He draws a parallel with the country’s pop-up shop culture, which can transform a street over night, and Korea’s rapid pace of change which, viewed from Europe, makes him feel far behind as well as far away.

A simple kimchi pancake is on the menu for Haribo Kimchi, its aroma filling the room in a show where Koo’s narrative is often sensory – such as the persimmon fruit trees he remembers from his youth. The theatregoers who take a seat at his bar are first given a somaek, a cocktail made with soju and beer, then several dishes including cold seaweed soup. As you’d expect from the theatrical cookery genre, which has included productions as different as Travis Alabanza’s Burgerz and Hannah Khalil’s My English Persian Kitchen, each item on the menu has a different emotional resonance – Koo likens it to a score of carefully chosen compositions. Seaweed, for example, has links with birthday traditions in Korea and with ocean myths.

That brings us to Koo’s unusual co-star: a robotic eel who slithers around the stage and even delivers a ballad. (A giant gummy bear and a snail break out in song too.) It’s not as random as it sounds – Koo says he was drawn to the way eels leave their birth home, journey afar, but “then go back to their home before they die”.

Haribo Kimchi, designed by Eunkyung Jeong (who is married to Koo) and with dramaturgy by their regular collaborator Dries Douibi, had its UK premiere at this summer’s Edinburgh international festival, where the audience invaded the stage for his end-of-show buffet. It’s not the first time Koo has found that mealtimes can make perfect metaphors for a show. In Korea, he says, “When we say hello, we always ask: ‘Did you have a good meal?’ Korean people call family sikku, which means ‘people who eat together’.” His earlier production Cuckoo, which he revived in Oslo, uses rice cookers as a symbol of both “economic imperialism and the pressure upon society”.

Cuckoo delves into the longterm impact of Korea’s late 90s financial crisis and its neoliberal shift after the International Monetary Fund intervened with a $58bn rescue package. The part played by US treasury secretary Robert Rubin in what Koo calls “economic imperialism” is given a catchy electro-pop tune to rival Bo Burnham’s Jeff Bezos takedown. Koo describes, in a show as angry and raw as Haribo Kimchi is gentle and warm, a severe spike in unemployment, inequality and isolation – “a generation without a future”, including an account of his close friend’s suicide.

Cuckoo is the name of Korea’s brand of ubiquitous talking rice cookers – Koo appears on stage with three of them which have been hacked so that they gripe at each other and even sing. Listening to an answerphone message from his father, Koo cradles one cooker as if it’s his own child. The show also has much of the poppy melancholy of Haribo Kimchi and blurs with performance art: in the climax, he tips a mound of rice from the cooker, steam rises, and he feverishly prepares it in portions – an act of control and division as much as cheffing.

His other shows take in linguistic colonisation: Lolling and Rolling is about the tongue surgery some South Koreans pursue in order to pronounce the English “R”. The History of Korean Western Theatre examines what you could call theatrical imperialism. “I studied at university in Korea and it was quite a conservative environment in terms of what theatre can be,” he says. In this classical western definition of drama, there was no room for a robotic eel or a chatty rice cooker and Koo is intent on putting tech on stage. “When we think about our contemporary world, it’s impossible to think and understand only with a human perspective. If we want to understand our time, then we have to think about different perspectives – nature, animals – and also technology like robotics.”

In his Oslo ceremony speech, Koo duly reflected on the irony of receiving an award named after a canonical figure such as Ibsen: “But he was also an artist who questioned the theatre and society of his own time.” His next project will grapple with another artform that has become “a force for change”: K-pop, whose fans have wielded the genre’s bangers and glow sticks as a form of political protest, notably against former President Yoon’s martial law attempt in 2024. It will be the first of Koo’s shows where he will not perform; the cast will comprise singers. “I want to examine our global society through the lens of K-pop,” he says. “It has strong power as a new form of pop culture … On the other hand, the industry has a really dark side.”

Theatre, for Koo, is an arena for us “to think together” he says. “This kind of solidarity is very important,” he adds. It’s drama as an act of breaking bread with the audience – or slurping cold seaweed soup.

GeneralTab.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
GeneralTab.text:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.

The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.

She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.

Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.

Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.

Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.

The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

GeneralTab.title: Man seriously injured in tiger attack at Yorkshire Wildlife Park
GeneralTab.text:
A man has been seriously injured after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have said.

South Yorkshire Police said it was called at 13:35 BST to reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster.

In a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

The park will remain closed for the remainder of the weekend, it added.

The force has confirmed the tiger "attacked the man and this has resulted in serious injury".

Officers were attempting to contact his family, it said.

"The tiger remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public," the force added.

The park was evacuated following the incident and officers remain at the scene.

Police have urged people not to share "distressing footage" of the incident.

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, was on a family day out when staff told them the park was being evacuated.

"We were in a lemur enclosure and somebody asked us to start leaving," she said. "Then, all of a sudden, we were being ushered further and further into the park."

Pelham said she had then heard what sounded like several gunshots.

"Then we saw a helicopter circling. That's when we started thinking, 'Oh, something's happened'."

She added: "There was big black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

GeneralTab.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
GeneralTab.text:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.

Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.

Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.

It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.

Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.

Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.

He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.

Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.

Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".

GeneralTab.title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
GeneralTab.text:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

GeneralTab.title: One more ex-banker jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
GeneralTab.text:
Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle.

The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor.

It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week.

Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day."

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Eighteen of these have now been acquitted.

Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction.

The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments.

They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019.

Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS.

The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans.

The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials.

Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice.

He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s".

In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit.

However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge.

All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws.

articles.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after failed execution
articles.text:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.

The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.

She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.

Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.

Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.

"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.

Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.

The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

articles.title: Man seriously injured in tiger attack at Yorkshire Wildlife Park
articles.text:
A man has been seriously injured after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have said.

South Yorkshire Police said it was called at 13:35 BST to reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster.

In a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

The park will remain closed for the remainder of the weekend, it added.

The force has confirmed the tiger "attacked the man and this has resulted in serious injury".

Officers were attempting to contact his family, it said.

"The tiger remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public," the force added.

The park was evacuated following the incident and officers remain at the scene.

Police have urged people not to share "distressing footage" of the incident.

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, was on a family day out when staff told them the park was being evacuated.

"We were in a lemur enclosure and somebody asked us to start leaving," she said. "Then, all of a sudden, we were being ushered further and further into the park."

Pelham said she had then heard what sounded like several gunshots.

"Then we saw a helicopter circling. That's when we started thinking, 'Oh, something's happened'."

She added: "There was big black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

articles.title: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
articles.text:

articles.title: How Ashe's real life inspired her TikTok hit Stop The Wedding
articles.text:
No songwriter is ever off duty. And for the US pop singer Ashe, that included her wedding day.

Last October, she was getting ready to tie the knot at a gorgeous hilltop ceremony in Nashville when inspiration struck.

As she watched her family gather, the musician flashed back to her first wedding, almost a decade earlier. The contrast was stark.

She's called that first marriage "horrifying". Her ex, who she met in college, was, she says, emotionally manipulative and psychologically abusive.

He had insisted on a beachfront wedding, which sounds romantic until you learn that Ashe has a fear of the ocean.

In the run-up, she had been tempted to call it off, but felt powerless to stand up for herself.

On her second wedding day, she realised the opposite was true.

"I'm in a happy, healthy relationship and I have total autonomy over my own life," says the singer, now in her early 30s.

"I thought, if this didn't feel right, I could totally put a halt to the whole thing. I definitely didn't have that first time around."

As she adjusted her veil and prepared to walk down the aisle, she filed that feeling away.

Two months later, and back at work, the idea resurfaced and a song spilled out.

Its name? Stop the Wedding.

It unfolds like a movie scene. Ashe pleads with her younger self to trust her instincts.

"You know how you really feel / You don't have to waste your life," she sings, as the wedding band stutters to an uncertain halt.

"Do I wish I'd had that advice at the time? 1,000 per cent," Ashe says.

"If someone had given me the insight that I was not stuck, and that I could run, I could have changed things sooner. Maybe not at the altar. Maybe weeks before – but it was something I really could have used."

What about the line where she pledges to "burn the wedding dress and run away"?

"I didn't burn my dress," she laughs, "but I did get into a bathtub with it for a photoshoot right after I left my ex-husband, which really ruined it!"

A native of San Jose, she grew up in a conservative household where the radio was permanently tuned to Christian stations.

It was her grandad who introduced her to rock music, playing Tom Petty and Bob Dylan on long road trips. By her teens, she was writing her own music.

After studying orchestral composition at Boston's Berklee College of Music, she moved to Nashville and quickly found work as a songwriter.

She scored an early credit on Demi Lovato's 2017 song You Don't Do It For Me Anymore; but slowly grew frustrated that other people were singing her words.

The decision to become Ashe, whose full name is Ashlyn Rae Willson, didn't happen overnight. She appeared as a featured vocalist on a handful of dance tracks before plunging into a solo career.

Her then-husband was not impressed.

"I remember him saying, '[After this] no-one's ever going to love you for you. Anyone you meet now is going to meet you as Ashe, and I met you before'.

"It was truly manipulative, and it kept me stuck. It kept me stuck for a long, long time."

It can't be a coincidence that a song she wrote after signing her divorce papers became her breakthrough hit.

Moral of The Story (key lyric: "you can think that you're in love / when you're really just in pain") was released in 2019, and hit one billion streams after appearing in the hit Netflix series To All the Boys: PS I Still Love You.

Ashe was suddenly playing bigger venues and duetting with Niall Horan, but work became all consuming.

When her brother died of an overdose in 2020, she was back on stage within a month.

"There was so much momentum and I was saying yes to far too many things," she reflects now.

"It got to a point where the idea of touring was giving me panic attacks, and I just couldn't stomach being Ashe, which is such a shame, because I'm her."

In 2023, she had a nervous breakdown and stepped away from showbusiness.

"I had to halt everything. I bought a house in Nashville, I gardened, I saw a therapist and I gave myself a chance to miss music."

Stop The Wedding sets the tone, with abrupt tempo changes that track Ashe's inner turmoil. Lasso The Moon is more whimsical, setting out the star's outlandish requirements for a new partner.

"God forbid I raise my standards," she laughs.

Love Bomb explores the psychology of a manipulative ex (guess who?); while Swan Lake is a comically villainous portrait of Ashe's possessiveness, complete with a Bugsy Malone chorus line.

It's a deliberately maximalist record, recalling the lush orchestrations of ELO and The Carpenters, with a nod to the revivalist pop of Ashe's friend Laufey.

"We were so bored of making music that's boring," she says.

"It scratches an itch for me as an artist to do something different and not meet the status quo."

The album ends back at her second wedding. The closing track focuses on the "real, true, constant love" she's found with musician John Clark Canada.

"You'll be my Tuesday night and my Sunday drive / And the last speech at my funeral," she sings.

Expanding on that idea, Ashe incorporates the ebullient sound of a New Orleans funeral band in the song's closing moments.

And the person they're burying is the disillusioned girl from Stop The Wedding.

Ashe's album, Girl of Your Dreams, is out on 16 October.

articles.title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
articles.text:
When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.

But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history.

"Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."

The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.

Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.

She says the whole process took its toll.

"I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.

Days before Aaliyah's 25th birthday, a large unmarked envelope landed on the doormat of her home, in Birmingham.

"I rip it open, thinking it's an early birthday present," she says.

But what was inside was the response to her data request - pages and pages of her family history, including some medical details she had been painstakingly trying to track down for years.

The documents contained upsetting information alluding to the reason she was taken into care, alongside court records and a personal letter from her social worker.

"They were just given to me in a completely nondescript pile, and they contained completely earth-shattering information, of which I don't think I have ever recovered from," she says.

Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns.

"My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know."

When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity.

Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history.

And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country.

The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more.

"Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available."

Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience.

For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk.

The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home".

But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions.

Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged.

Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris.

"There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family."

A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted.

The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia.

While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia.

After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family.

He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested.

Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot".

"There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan."

A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026.

Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at.

"Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said.

He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health.

"We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said.

Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations.

None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information.

But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care.

NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party".

But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care.

For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored.

Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place.

"She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'".

A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line

articles.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago - why are they resuming now?
articles.text:
They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.

By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.

That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.

The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.

That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.

The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be live-streamed.

"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.

University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.

"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.

He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.

"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.

It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.

With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".

Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.

The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."

But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"

Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.

Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US.

"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."

"I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."

The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday.

Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen." He added that "if it's through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it".

Hours later, President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.

The president did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution.

"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

articles.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
articles.text:
If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.

The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.

But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an £7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.

Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.

The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).

What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.

Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.

Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.

"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.

A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."

Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".

But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate.

"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."

Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.

Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.

Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."

The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.

Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.

She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.

Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".

"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."

Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".

"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."

The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.

The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.

It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.

Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.

"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.

While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.

"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.

Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.

But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.

Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.

There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.

For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.

Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana

articles.title: Ukraine war: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people
articles.text:
Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, officials said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city on Saturday morning. At least 16 others were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks on Zaporizhzhia were Russia expressing "its thanks" for a deal announced by US President Donald Trump last night easing sanctions on Moscow to import Russian diesel.

He added that 13 other regions had come under attack overnight, arguing this demonstrated Russia took "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting".

Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes in Zaporizhzhia show an apartment block mostly destroyed.

"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television from the scene.

She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.

The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.

Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."

articles.title: Several injured in fresh attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport
articles.text:
Several people have been injured in another attack on an international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, authorities say, days after Yemen's Houthis claimed to have carried out similar strikes on the hub.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were suspended on Saturday after the attack, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority said in a statement.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to news agency Reuters, citing an eyewitness.

The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport" and urged American citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.

The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudis including a pilot were killed in two attacks on the airport by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior. Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.

A source at a local hospital told AFP that dozens of people had been wounded in Saturday's attack.

"I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running," an eyewitness who said they had been at gate 401 in the domestic terminal told the news agency.

Western embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens away from the airport.

Several Gulf airlines said they had cancelled their flights to and from the airport. with Kuwait Airways citing the "security situation" there.

All flights to Riyadh have either been diverted or cancelled, aviation tracker Flightradar shows.

Doctors had been asked to report to hospitals to address the situation, a medical source told AFP.

"We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'," the medical source told the agency.

The suspected attack comes during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.

The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.

The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

But the informal truce began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

articles.title: CJP at Jantar Mantar: 'Cockroach' group says leaders detained at Delhi protest
articles.text:
Hundreds of protesters have been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) calling for electoral reforms.

The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke - who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches" - was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.

Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.

Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.

The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.

It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.

Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.

But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.

The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.

The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.

Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."

He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.

The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.

The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.

Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"

The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.

In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

articles.title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
articles.text:
A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in a third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.

The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw, police told news agencies PAP and AP.

It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker.

A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.

Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition was not life-threatening.

Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had gone in to submit enrolment documents, were also injured, Poland's state news agency reported.

Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggested that she did not know the three victims.

Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had detained 76 people after deploying to schools across the country.

"When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.

Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.

On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.

A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

articles.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
articles.text:
Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.

The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.

"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.

The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.

The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".

The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.

articles.title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
articles.text:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

articles.title: One more ex-banker jailed for rigging rates has conviction overturned
articles.text:
Another former banker sentenced in one of the biggest scandals of the financial crisis has had his conviction overturned following a long-running legal battle.

The Court of Appeal has quashed the conviction of Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who went to prison in 2018 for "manipulating" the benchmark interest rate, Euribor.

It comes after the same UK court overturned five convictions of ex-Barclays bankers in the rate rigging trials earlier this week.

Bittar, who watched proceedings via video link from Switzerland because he was not granted a visa to attend court, told the BBC: "I have waited a very, very long time for this day."

The financial crisis began in 2008, sending huge economic shockwaves across the world and triggering recessions in many countries.

There was a public backlash against bankers, held by many to be responsible for the crisis, while the financial sector was protected by taxpayer-funded bailouts.

The Libor scandal erupted in 2012, when it was discovered that at the outbreak of the financial crisis, banks had been misrepresenting their positions during the process of setting the lending rate, helping to boost profits and mask difficulties.

Some 19 City traders were convicted in the US and UK between 2015 and 2019 across nine criminal trials held in London and New York.

Eighteen of these have now been acquitted.

Only one former trader in the world now remains convicted: former Barclays trader Peter Johnson, who was also one of the original whistleblowers in the interest rate rigging scandal. He pleaded guilty on advice that he had little chance at winning at trial. The court confirmed that he too has now applied to appeal against his conviction.

The news has already prompted lawyers and senior politicians to press for the Bank of England and the Treasury to release all their records about their own roles in interest rate 'rigging' during the financial crisis, amid concerns raised of a cover-up of the role of central banks and governments.

They launched fresh appeals against their jail sentences following a Supreme Court ruling last year that acquitted Tom Hayes, the first to be jailed for 'rigging' interest rates in 2015, and Carlo Palombo, jailed in 2019.

Tom Hayes, who was initially sentenced to 14 years, reduced on appeal to 11, is now seeking damages from his former employer UBS.

The traders were among 37 City traders and brokers prosecuted for "manipulating" the interest rate benchmarks Libor and Euribor, which track the cost of borrowing cash between the banks and have been used to set the interest rates on millions of mortgages and commercial loans.

The BBC has uncovered evidence of a much larger, state-led 'rigging' of interest rates, under pressure from central banks and governments across the world. Evidence implicating Downing Street and the Bank of England was suppressed throughout the criminal trials.

Former Conservative cabinet minister David Davis told the BBC the innocent traders had been the victims of a series of miscarriages of justice.

He said the people exonerated this week and before were "the victims of a scapegoating exercise which arose as a result of the government's own misbehaviour in lowballing [falsely understating] Libor interest rates themselves, in order to try and rescue the economy after their own self-induced crash in the late 2000s".

In 2015, during the first trial for interest rate 'rigging', of former UBS trader Hayes, Mr Justice Jeremy Cooke decided as a matter of law that any attempt to influence the rates could not be lawful, and that any rate influenced by commercial interest must automatically be false. Judges in the subsequent eight trials followed suit.

However, in July 2025, the Supreme Court decided that all the judges had erred, misdirecting juries that it was wrong as a matter of law. Instead, whether the requests were right or wrong was properly a matter of fact for the jury to decide, not the judge.

All convictions in the United States were overturned in 2022 after an appeal court ruled that there was insufficient evidence that the traders' requests had broken any rules or laws.

articles.title: How soon into dating should you reveal your salary?
articles.text:
You know their favourite restaurant, what happened with their ex and their most embarrassing childhood story. But do you know how much your partner earns?

Money remains one of dating's trickier conversations. Bring it up too early and it can sound like you're sizing up their bank balance. But leave it too long and you could be planning a future with someone without knowing much about their finances at all.

We spoke to 20-somethings in New York City to see if there was a sweet spot for when to talk salaries.

Willa Morton, 25, says she doesn't think couples necessarily need to reveal their salaries at all.

"It's just a number and you can gauge how much someone makes based on the way they live and how much they spend," she says.

Willa, who works in tech sales, has talked to her boyfriend about not earning very much herself but hasn't asked him for a figure in return.

He's a company founder and, though his income varies, she knows that he earns more than she does.

"He's more free-spending whereas I'm always saying, 'That's too expensive, that costs too much, we don't need to spend that.'"

Their dates typically cost around $200 (£150) and he usually pays, while she picks up smaller bills such as coffees.

"It's an unspoken rule that he will pick up the bigger bills."

For many, there's a fairly clear dividing line as to when you talk about salary, spending habits and debt and that's when you become an official couple.

Alexa Ludato, 25, who works in insurance, says she'd only have the conversation when she was official with someone.

Before then, she would "like to have an idea of what their job is, but not how much they make".

Her friend, Vik Sunderaj, 22, agrees. "You should only discuss it once you get into a serious relationship."

He thinks a salary question on the first few dates is "a little crazy".

"If they asked, I would be honest, but I wouldn't bring it up," he says. And if his date really wanted to know his salary, "it probably means they wouldn't be the right person for me".

Becoming official doesn't necessarily mean swapping payslips though.

Insurance worker Emily Moretta, 26, has been with her boyfriend for two years and says they still haven't explicitly told each other their salaries and "he doesn't know how much I make".

She assumes he probably has a rough idea, but says neither has ever felt the need to ask.

"Maybe down the line we would, when it gets more serious," she says, adding that they would have to be at the stage of moving in together before talking about it.

articles.title: 'Add me on WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
articles.text:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.

But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.

The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.

The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.

Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.

Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.

"Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam," he said.

"They would either put you through to a fake job listing, which might involve some form of money muling. It could look like a completely legitimate job, or something ad hoc, but they might pass criminal funds through your account which can lead to terrible consequences.

"It could also be a simple phishing exercise - criminals send out these messages, and what they really want to know is who's picking up, who's active - that information can be resold on the dark web.

"The possibilities are endless. At the end of the day this is a criminal that has reached out to you and they're trying to defraud you in some way shape or form."

Andy Curry, the ICO's head of criminal investigations, told the BBC he believed the calls were coming from abroad.

"We are trying to find who is behind this, why they're doing it and the impact it's having on members of the public," he said.

The number of complaints received by the ICO would only be a small proportion of the totals affected, he said.

"We think there are probably millions of people who are receiving these messages, which appear to us to be largely indiscriminate.

"I've had them, my colleague who's leading the investigation has had them. It's likely to be tip of the iceberg."

articles.title: Firmus: Nvidia-backed data centre firm scraps IPO as AI valuation concerns deepen
articles.text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) data centre company Firmus has scrapped its plans for what would have been one of Australia's biggest-ever stock market listings.

The Nvidia-backed firm said it had made the decision due to "recent market volatility and prevailing market conditions" and that going public would not be in the company or shareholders' best interests.

Firmus had initially announced plans for a stock market debut that valued the company at more than $30bn (£22.65bn).

One investment firm told the BBC that it had decided not to take part in the initial public offering (IPO) over concerns about its valuation.

"Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options. We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress," the company said.

Firmus builds and operates liquid-cooled data centres, or what it calls "AI factories", for clients including OpenAI and Meta.

It has operations in Australia, Singapore and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region.

The company's backers include Nvidia and major investment firms Blackstone and Jane Street.

Blackstone declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia and Jane Street have also been contacted for comment.

The decision by Firmus to scrap its stock market listing comes as investors and industry analysts have raised concerns about the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into AI as the prospects for long-term returns remain unclear.

UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among the institutional investors that decided not take part in the IPO.

"We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation," UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce said in an update to investors.

He also said UniSuper was concerned that Firmus would have to go further into debt to fund its growth plans.

"It's disappointing. The [Australian Securities Exchange] needs new stories and this could have been one if it was correctly priced," Pearce told the BBC.

This kind of listing is a test of how willing companies are to keep "ploughing money" into AI, said Phillip Wool, chief research officer from Rayliant Investment Research.

Investors in Firmus would be buying into a company that is still in its early stages and is likely to need to borrow large sums of money, Wool said.

"It's more like a bet on a dream", he added.

Australia has become an attractive destination for data centre investment, thanks to the country's abundant clean energy, natural gas supplies and land availability.
